text: A ServiceNow Administrator job posting lists things like managing users and groups, maintaining the service catalog, and supporting platform upgrades. All of that is real, but it undersells how reactive the actual week usually is.

Course 3 taught you how ACLs, roles, and groups work as a system. In a real admin seat, a lot of your time is spent applying that knowledge to specific, urgent situations: a manager says someone can't see records they should see, a catalog item is routing approvals to the wrong person, or a scheduled job quietly stopped running. The administrator is who gets paged when the platform itself isn't behaving as expected — not a business process on top of it, the platform.

Four things fill most of the real calendar. Access management — ACLs, roles, and groups — is course 3 and course 10 applied continuously, not set up once and forgotten. Catalog and workflow maintenance means keeping items and flows working as the business changes around them; something that worked for a year can quietly break when a referenced group or field changes elsewhere. Upgrades and patching are calendar-driven: testing in a sub-production instance, then coordinating the real production window. And platform tickets — a form that won't save, a notification that won't fire — draw on the troubleshooting instincts course 2 built around the data model and business rules.

Administrators don't own ITSM process decisions — a change manager or problem manager does — but they're the ones who turn those decisions into working configuration. A process owner asks for approvals to skip a step under a specific condition; the administrator has to scope that change precisely enough that it doesn't quietly break the rest of an approval chain that already works. That translation skill only really develops by doing it repeatedly.

One more honest note: the title means different things at different company sizes. At a smaller organization, admin work often blends with scoped development because there's no headcount to split the functions. At a larger enterprise, it's usually specialized and separate. Read the actual responsibilities in a posting, not just the title. Next up: what the ServiceNow Developer role actually looks like day to day.
